item.title: Blocks with ownership: a novel approach to CPU and GPU memory in C++
item.description:
Introduction

Every C and C++ programmer knows the contract: malloc(size) returns a pointer, and free(ptr) takes it back. The size is missing from the second half, free gets only the pointer.

In case you’re unfamiliar with how allocators work there is a great short introduction video about it, you can watch it here:

malloc() is lying to you. Find out why, and how the illusion works! pic.twitter.com/pUjYVEqBSD

— Dave W Plummer (@davepl1968) May 15, 2026

Most people visualize allocation as something like this:

You call char* buffer = (char*)malloc(1); and you get:

But actually it looks like this:

Memory header and footer are usually allocator metadata which is used for allocator operations, optionally some memory tracking, and some mechanism to detect memory errors. Memory footer is not common unless allocator has some memory corruption detection mechanisms.

Memory header is usually where malloc stores the size of the block in order for free(ptr) to work. The allocator knew how much memory it handed out, the caller knew how much it asked for, but free gets only the pointer, so the allocator has to write the size down somewhere, usually in a header in front of the block, and find it again later. std::allocator passes the size back, but the rest is the same: an allocation is a bare pointer, and everything else about it, how big it really is, how it’s aligned, who allocated it, lives somewhere else.

In 2015 Andrei Alexandrescu proposed a different contract: an allocation is not a pointer, it’s a block, the pointer and the size together. The allocator returns the block, the caller keeps it, and hands it back when it’s done. Once allocators speak in blocks they can be small, do one thing, and be composed into larger ones.

This post is about bx::Blk, an implementation of that idea taken further than the talk. The block also knows which allocator it came from, it can’t be copied or freed twice by accident, when it’s invalid it says why, and it describes GPU memory the same way it describes CPU memory. On top of it there is a set of composable allocators, allocation debugging, memory tracking and a general purpose heap.

History of composable allocators

Composition came from C first. Kiem‑Phong Vo’s Vmalloc (1996) splits an allocator into a method, how blocks are handed out (Vmbest, Vmpool, Vmlast), and a discipline, where raw memory comes from (Vmdcsystem for mmap, sbrk or Win32). Any method works with any discipline, and debugging is just another method: Vmdebug checks for overruns and double frees, Vmprofile records usage.

Emery Berger, Benjamin Zorn and Kathryn McKinley’s Heap Layers (PLDI 2001) brought it to C++. Each layer is a template that inherits from the layer below, and an allocator is a stack of layers. Composed allocators matched hand‑written ones, and Hoard and DieHard are built from it. The same year Andrei Alexandrescu’s Modern C++ Design introduced policy‑based design, the mechanism his allocators would use fourteen years later, and Loki’s small object allocator.

Also in 2001, Jeff Bonwick and Jonathan Adams added magazines and vmem to the Solaris slab allocator. Magazines are per‑CPU caches of free blocks. Vmem allocates arbitrary resources, ranges of integers, so it never touches what it manages.

Game developers kept running into the limits of std::allocator. Paul Pedriana’s N2271 (2007) says std::allocator was the largest reason EA wrote EASTL.

Alexandrescu’s talk

Alexandrescu presented composable allocators at CppCon 2015, in the “std::allocator Is to Allocation what std::vector Is to Vexation” talk:

In the talk he introduces two main ideas:

  • Allocation returns Blk { void* ptr; size_t length; }. The allocator says how much it gave, the caller keeps it and hands it back, and the allocator doesn’t have to store the size.

  • Allocators are small parts with the same interface, allocate, deallocate, expand, reallocate and owns, put together with templates. FallbackAllocator<Primary, Fallback> asks Primary::owns to decide who frees a block. Segregator splits by size, Bucketizer makes size classes, AffixAllocator adds a prefix or suffix for metadata, and StatsCollector counts.

Alexandrescu implemented the whole thing in D as std.experimental.allocator, released with D 2.069 in November 2015, where a block is a void[] slice. It is the most complete implementation of the talk, and it is still in experimental.

In C++ there are AllocatorBuilder, allocators and KTL, which reproduce the building blocks from the talk, and foonathan/memory, which passes memory_block between allocator layers and hands users plain pointers. The standard took one piece: allocate_at_least in C++23 returns { ptr, count }.

On the GPU side, AMD’s Vulkan Memory Allocator and D3D12 Memory Allocator have virtual blocks, and Sebastian Aaltonen’s OffsetAllocator is TLSF for offsets. They hand out offsets into memory the CPU can’t touch and keep metadata outside of it, each with its own API, separate from how the same program allocates CPU memory.

bx::Blk

The Blk from the talk is two fields, struct Blk { void* ptr; size_t length; }, and it’s a plain value. bx::Blk keeps the idea, the caller holds the block and hands it back, and changes almost everything else about it.

Layout

 1struct Blk                            // 24 bytes, 64-bit layout
 2{
 3    uint64_t ptr;                     // pointer, or offset into GPU memory
 4
 5    uint64_t size            : 40;    // size of block, up to 1TiB
 6    uint64_t log2Alignment   :  5;    // alignment of block
 7    uint64_t cpuAccessible   :  1;    // can CPU read and write this memory?
 8    uint64_t allocatorOp     :  3;    // what the last operation did
 9    uint64_t allocatorHandle :  8;    // which allocator returned the block
10
11    uint32_t bookKeeping;             // private data of the allocator
12    uint16_t slotIndex;               // routing inside of composed allocator
13    uint16_t unused0;
14
15    uint32_t locationIdx;             // only with memory tracking, 32 bytes
16    uint32_t unused1;
17};

What the fields are for, compared to pointer and length in the talk:

  • ptr is 64 bits on every platform, including 32‑bit ones, because it’s not always a pointer. For GPU memory it’s an offset.

  • size is the size the allocator actually gave, which can be more than what was asked for.

  • log2Alignment is there because alignment is something the caller knows at allocation, and has to repeat on every resize and free. Now it’s in the block.

  • allocatorOp says what happened to the block last: no‑operation, alias, allocate, free, grow, realign, or truncate. There is one entry point, realloc(blk, size, alignment), and the caller can tell if the block grew in place or moved.

  • allocatorHandle is the allocator the block came from.

  • bookKeeping and slotIndex belong to allocators. Metadata that an allocator would write into a header in front of the memory can live in the block, which matters when the memory is on the GPU and there is nowhere to write the header.

Unique pointer without automatic release

This is the largest change in behavior. In the talk a block is a plain struct, and nothing stops this:

1Blk a = allocator.allocate(100);
2Blk b = a;               // copy of metadata
3allocator.deallocate(a);
4allocator.deallocate(b); // double free, and `b` looked completely valid

The same happens when a block is resized and the old copy is kept around, the old copy has the wrong pointer or the wrong size, and it’s the caller’s job to never use it.

bx::Blk behaves like std::unique_ptr, there is always only one owner of the block:

  • It can’t be copied, only moved, and moving invalidates the source.

  • Every function that changes a block takes it as Blk&& and returns the result. The block that went in is invalid when the function returns. If a resize fails, the original block is what comes back, marked as no‑operation.

  • It’s [[nodiscard]], the result can’t be dropped on the floor.

In code:

1bx::Blk blk = bx::alloc(allocator, 100);
2blk = bx::realloc(bx::move(blk), 200); // old block is gone, there is only
3                                       // the new one
4blk = bx::free(bx::move(blk) );        // `blk` is now invalid, reason: freed
5
6bx::Blk copy = blk;                    // doesn't compile
7bx::free(blk);                         // doesn't compile

Unlike std::unique_ptr, Blk doesn’t free memory when it goes out of scope. Allocation and release stay explicit, there are no frees hidden behind a closing brace, and without a destructor Blk is trivially relocatable, 24 bytes that containers and allocators can move around with memcpy. What unique_ptr gives for free at scope exit is done by containers that own a block: ArrayT, HashMapT, UniquePtrT.

Forgetting to free is caught another way. With memory tracking turned on, Blk gets a destructor that doesn’t free, it asserts if the block that’s going away still owns memory, and reports where that block was allocated. A leak is reported at the place where the block is lost, not as a list of leaked pointers at exit.

When more than one piece of code needs to look at the same block, the copy has to be asked for: Blk(Copy, blk) makes a non‑owning alias. It’s marked as AllocatorOp::Alias, it can’t be resized or freed, and it’s not counted as a leak.

Memory tracking changes the size of Blk, so Blk lives in an inline namespace named after BX_CONFIG_MEMORY_TRACKING. Code built with tracking and code built without it doesn’t link, instead of crashing at runtime.

The block knows its allocator

In the talk the allocator is not part of the block. The caller has to remember which allocator a block came from, and composed allocators find the owner by asking each part owns(blk).

bx::Blk carries an 8‑bit handle of the allocator that returned it. free(blk) and realloc(blk, ...) don’t take an allocator argument, there is no header in front of the memory, and no lookup by address.

The handle is 8 bits because it has to fit into the block next to the size and alignment, and that makes 256 handles. A handle is an index into a table of allocators, so getting from a block to its allocator is one read from an array. Allocators get a handle when they’re created, and handle 0 is the process default, which is the heap until it’s set to something else with setDefaultAllocatorBlk.

256 sounds small, but handles are for allocators, not for allocations, and a program has few allocators. The whole bx heap takes about 12. The limit is also on allocators that are alive at the same time, not on how many are created: when an allocator is destroyed its handle is released, and released handles are reused in turn. Running out of handles is an assert, and code that creates and destroys allocators all the time should reset them instead.

Reuse of handles is why an allocator has to outlive every block it returned. A block that is still around after its allocator is gone carries a handle that sooner or later belongs to another allocator. With memory tracking, destroying an allocator that has live blocks is an assert.

Some allocators are never destroyed, they live as long as the process. Those can be marked with setAllocatorPermanent, and a permanent handle is never given to another allocator. That handle means the same allocator for as long as the process runs, so the pointer to the allocator can be cached instead of looked up. The heap marks its own allocators as permanent. The default handle is not permanent, because it can be pointed at another allocator.

Containers get smaller because of it. They take a one byte AllocatorHandle instead of an allocator pointer, and ArrayT or UniquePtrT store nothing but their Blk.

Invalid blocks say why

A null pointer says that something failed. An invalid Blk says what: allocation failed, no block large enough (but smaller ones are available), resize failed, realign failed, not supported, or the block was freed. A block that was freed is distinguishable from one that was never allocated.

One entry point

The allocator interface in the talk has allocate, deallocate, reallocate and expand. A bx allocator has one function, realloc(blk, size, alignment). An invalid block going in is an allocation, size 0 is a free, anything else is a resize, and allocatorOp in the block that comes back says which one happened.

The functions users call are built on top of it, and each comes in three forms:

  • tryAlloc, tryRealloc report failure through Error*, and the caller has to deal with it.

  • alloc, realloc, free stop on failure.

  • Unchecked variants skip the checks, for hot paths where the caller guarantees the preconditions.

Not all code can hold a 24 byte block. For code that can only keep a pointer there are allocPtr, reallocPtr, freePtr and BX_NEW_PTR/deletePtr, which store the Blk in a header in front of the pointer. It’s what malloc does, but only where it’s asked for.

Block allocators and old pointer based AllocatorI can’t be confused. Passing one where the other is expected doesn’t compile.

Allocators

Allocators are plain classes without virtual functions, composed with templates, so the calls between the parts inline. The parts:

  • Memory sources. SystemMemoryAllocator takes pages from the operating system. PageReserveAllocator reserves address space for each block and commits pages as the block grows, so the block grows in place and never moves. FixedCapacityAllocatorT hands out one block from inline storage.

  • Managing a region. FirstFitAllocatorT, BitArrayAllocatorT and TwoLevelSegregatedFitAllocatorT (TLSF) for general use. FrameRingAllocatorT for transient per‑frame allocations with multiple frames in flight, DoubleEndedStackAllocatorT for a stack that grows from both ends.

  • Composition. ThresholdAllocatorT sends blocks up to a size to one allocator and the rest to another, it’s the segregator from the talk. OverflowAllocatorT uses the secondary allocator when the primary is out of memory, the talk’s fallback. MoreCoreAllocatorT takes memory from the secondary and adds it to the primary instead.

  • Threads. MutexAllocatorT puts a lock around any allocator. ThreadLocalAllocatorT gives each thread its own instance, and blocks can be freed on any thread. ThreadCacheAllocatorT adds a per‑thread cache of small blocks, with Bonwick’s magazines.

  • Sensitive data. SecureAllocatorT wraps any allocator and clears the memory of freed and resized blocks, so keys and passwords don’t stay behind in memory that was given back.

  • Adapters. ImplementAllocatorBlkInterfaceT puts any of them behind the virtual AllocatorBlkI when a block allocator has to cross an API boundary, and IntrusiveBlkAllocatorT exposes a block allocator as the old pointer based AllocatorI.

First fit and TLSF don’t own the memory they manage. Memory is added to them and removed from them as slabs (addSlab, removeUnusedSlab), and that is the same interface whether the slab is RAM or a GPU heap.

CPU and GPU memory

In the talk a block is CPU memory, void*, and allocators are free to write into memory they manage. In bx::Blk the cpuAccessible bit says if ptr can be dereferenced. When it can’t, ptr is an offset, allocators keep all metadata outside of the memory, and debug features that touch memory are skipped.

That’s all it takes for the same allocators and the same composition to work on both. TLSF, first fit, or frame ring sub‑allocate a GPU heap the same way they sub‑allocate RAM. bgfx does exactly this:

  • D3D12 and Vulkan renderers have one TwoLevelSegregatedFitAllocatorT per kind of memory. Each ID3D12Heap or VkDeviceMemory is added as a slab the CPU can’t access, with the index of the heap in the upper bits of ptr. Heaps that are no longer used are removed and given back to the driver.

  • Dynamic vertex and index buffers are ranges of a larger GPU buffer, handed out by FirstFitAllocatorT, not TLSF. It’s a different allocator behind the same slab interface, each GPU buffer is added as a slab.

This is how a VkDeviceMemory goes in and an allocation comes out in bgfx’s Vulkan renderer, simplified:

 1// Device memory is added as a slab. Index of the slab is in the upper 32 bits
 2// of `ptr`, and the block is marked as not accessible by the CPU.
 3allocator.addSlab(
 4      bx::Blk(uint64_t(slabIdx + 1) << 32
 5    , size
 6    , 0
 7    , false
 8    , bx::AllocatorOp::Allocate
 9    ) );
10
11// Allocation is a block. Which device memory, and the offset into it,
12// are both in `ptr`.
13bx::Blk blk = allocator.alloc(requirements.size, requirements.alignment);
14
15const uint16_t slabIdx = uint16_t( (blk.ptr >> 32) - 1);
16const uint32_t offset  = uint32_t(blk.ptr);

Nothing is written into the device memory, what TLSF needs to free the block later is in the block’s bookKeeping.

Memory tracking and debugging

With BX_CONFIG_MEMORY_TRACKING every allocation records where in the source it was made. The location is a defaulted argument of alloc, like std::source_location, so there are no macros at call sites. Each location keeps the number of live blocks and bytes, their peaks, the number of operations, and the call stack of the first allocation from it, and all locations can be enumerated at any time. The block points to its location, which is how the leak assert in ~Blk knows what to report. With tracking compiled out Blk goes back to 24 bytes with no destructor.

Debugging tools are allocators too, and they’re added by composition, around any allocator and at any level:

  • StatsAllocatorT counts bytes, blocks and operations, and is thread safe.

  • DebugClearAllocatorT fills new memory with 0xcd and freed memory with 0xdd.

  • DebugStompAllocator places each block against a guard page, after the block to catch overruns or before it to catch underruns, so out of bounds access and use after free trap at the instruction that did it (see Memory Stomp Allocator).

General purpose heap from the same parts

bx::malloc, realloc, alignedAlloc, free and usableSize run on a heap composed from the same block allocators. It’s a test of the whole idea: if composition from blocks had a cost, this is where it would show.

The heap has three modes, picked with setHeap:

  • Throughput. Threads own their pages.

  • Footprint. Threads share pages, and thread caches are bounded.

  • Balanced, the default. Blocks up to 8KiB come from pages owned by the thread, larger ones from shared pages.

Where the heap gets its memory from is also an allocator, set with setHeapUpstream.

Performance

All bx results below are from the balanced heap, which is the default. The throughput and footprint modes are not represented.

mimalloc‑bench

mimalloc‑bench is the benchmark that matters the most, because it’s based on reality. It runs real, familiar open source programs, redis, rocksdb, lean, espresso, cfrac, a Linux kernel build, next to the allocator stress tests, with each allocator loaded as the malloc of the process.

For each test an allocator gets the best result divided by its own, and the score is the geometric mean over all tests times 100, so 100 means the best on every test. Overall is time and memory weighted equally:

allocator time memory overall
mimalloc 1.8.2 90.0 82.0 85.9
snmalloc 0.7.6 90.0 69.8 79.2
bx 83.9 74.7 79.2
rpmalloc 2.0.1 82.9 70.9 76.7
mimalloc 2.1.2 84.5 68.1 75.9
glibc 2.39 61.4 81.2 70.6
jemalloc 5.4.0 77.1 61.7 69.0
mimalloc 3.6.0 87.2 45.8 63.2
tcmalloc (gperftools 2.18) 67.1 55.7 61.1

bx is in the leading group. It’s 1.37x faster than glibc, about 7% behind mimalloc 1.8 and snmalloc, about even with mimalloc 2 and 3 and rpmalloc, and ahead of jemalloc and tcmalloc. Only glibc and mimalloc 1.8 use less memory overall. It ties for the fastest on the kernel build, and trails the most on small block churn, where sh6bench is about 2x behind the fastest.

rpmalloc‑benchmark

rpmalloc‑benchmark is synthetic. Threads do nothing but allocate and free blocks of random sizes, and hand some of them to other threads to free. A program that only allocates doesn’t exist, so the differences it shows are much larger than what a real program would see, and it should be read as a stress test of the allocator and not as a prediction. It’s useful for comparing against platform allocators, because it runs everywhere. Three ranges of block sizes at 1, 4 and 8 threads:

platform platform allocator bx is faster by
Windows, Ryzen 9 7950X Windows heap 1.6–54x
Linux, i9‑9900K glibc 2.39 2.6–4.7x
macOS, Apple M4 libmalloc 3.1–9.1x
iPhone 16e, A18 libmalloc 4.2–8.5x
iPhone 17 Pro Max, A19 Pro libmalloc 3.6–15x
Pixel 9a, Tensor G4 Scudo 3.9–77x

Peak memory is close to even, except on Linux where glibc uses 4–14% less. Against the other allocators on Windows, scored the same way as above, bx gets 90.5 for speed and 86.8 for memory, rpmalloc 75.5 and 70.7, mimalloc 60.0 and 83.7, snmalloc 57.0 and 79.8, tcmalloc 48.8 and 69.5.

GPU sub‑allocation

bx allocators against Vulkan Memory Allocator and D3D12 Memory Allocator, both as virtual blocks over a 256MiB virtual heap, with three workloads: churn of live blocks, transient blocks of one frame, and three frames in flight. For 256 allocations and 256 frees of each, bx TLSF, the one bgfx uses, takes 25.6µs in total, VMA 32.1µs and D3D12MA 31.4µs.

Conclusion

Blocks are not new, composable allocators are not new, and neither is any single allocator described here. Blocks with a size come from Alexandrescu’s talk, composition from Vmalloc and Heap Layers, and TLSF, magazines and GPU sub‑allocators all existed before. What is novel is what bx::Blk does with the block. As far as I know, no other implementation makes the block the single owner of its memory, puts the allocator into the block, or manages CPU and GPU memory with the same blocks and the same allocators, and none has built a general purpose malloc replacement out of blocks.

None of this is paid for with performance. On real programs the general purpose heap composed from these parts is in the same group as allocators that do nothing else, and 1.37x faster than glibc.

It’s not an experiment. It landed in bx, and bgfx’s D3D12 and Vulkan renderers sub‑allocate GPU memory with the same allocators.

item.title: Shader compiler survey
item.description:
Introduction

Over the years of maintaining shaderc I formed an opinion of how a shader compiler should look. Not the language, I don’t care much about the language (as long as it is C‑like 😉), but the thing itself: what goes in, what comes out, and how much of it I am allowed to touch. I made a list of what I think an ideal shader compiler looks like, shaped by offline and embedded use: platforms that do not allow compiling shaders at runtime, shipping optimized IR, keeping the executable small when a shader compiler is used at runtime, and being able to inject or skip stages. Then I went through what exists today, checked each one against the list, and benchmarked them all.

The ideal shader compiler

1. Text in, text out. The compiler must take text, lex and parse it, run some optimizations (or not), and be able to print text again. This is the glsl‑optimizer case: the driver is bad at optimizing, the API accepts only source, and I want at least basic passes done before the shader ships.

2. Any proprietary compiler can be attached at the end. On NDA (a.k.a. video game console) platforms compiling or generating code at runtime is not an option, and the platform compiler might sign the binary with an algorithm nobody outside knows. The last stage has to be replaceable with a black box.

3. Any part of it can be skipped. Including all of it. When I need a feature the compiler doesn’t support, and there is no time to add it properly, I want to go straight through to the back‑end compiler instead of bolting something on the side.

4. Things can be injected at any stage. I must be able to get at the IR between stages and transform it into what I need.

5. It is configurable. Everything I don’t need for the target I’m building for should be strippable, and the binary should get smaller when I strip it.

6. It is a library. Embeddable, and not structured as a command line tool that happens to have a main() you can call. Can go from text to shader binary. Or could be limited, where we skip lexing, parsing and optimization and just convert IR to target shader binary. “Embeddable” in this context also means that shader compiler should not dominate binary size of executable if it’s embedded. If we have 100MiB library that gets linked with 1MiB executable, that is not really “embeddable”.

7. The IR is serializable. So that optimized shader IR can be shipped, and translated/emitted for the specific backend at runtime. This doesn’t work everywhere, but where it does it’s a nice feature.

8. The IR can be assembled at runtime, without the compiler. If generating a shader is simple, and there is nothing to gain from optimization passes, I should be able to emit IR directly and link only the back‑end. This is a binary size optimization.

9. It runs where I build. It must produce shaders the API can ingest from any major desktop OS: Windows, Linux, and macOS.

10. It should be fast. Even if fast means reentrant and have to use multiple threads to achieve high speed when compiling multiple shaders. Compiling multiple shaders is not dependent on each other, so a shader compiler should not force sequential compiling.

Nothing on this list is exotic. None of it is impossible or unheard of; it is how LLVM describes itself:

The LLVM Project is a collection of modular and reusable compiler and toolchain technologies.

The contenders

  • FXC, d3dcompiler_47.dll. HLSL to DXBC, for Direct3D 11.
  • DXC, dxcompiler.dll. HLSL to DXIL for Direct3D 12, or to SPIR‑V.
  • Metal compiler, metal. Metal Shading Language to AIR, for Metal.
  • Glslang+SPIRV‑Tools+SPIRV‑Cross. The Khronos stack: GLSL or HLSL to SPIR‑V, an optimizer, and SPIR‑V back to GLSL, ESSL, HLSL or MSL. Counted as one compiler because nobody uses just one of them.
  • Tint, from Dawn. WGSL or SPIR‑V in; WGSL, SPIR‑V, HLSL, MSL or GLSL out.
  • Naga, from wgpu. WGSL, SPIR‑V or GLSL in; WGSL, SPIR‑V, HLSL, MSL or GLSL out.
  • NIR, from Mesa. The IR every Mesa driver compiles through: SPIR‑V or GLSL in, an optimizer, and next to the hardware back‑ends, writers for SPIR‑V, DXIL and MSL.
  • Slang. Slang or HLSL in; SPIR‑V, HLSL, MSL, WGSL or GLSL out, and DXIL through DXC.

How they stack up against the list. The last row counts a plain yes as a point and anything qualified as partly:

FXC DXC Metal Khronos stack Tint Naga NIR Slang
1. Text in, text out no no no yes yes, no optimizer yes, no optimizer GLSL in, MSL out, inside a driver yes
2. Proprietary back‑end is one is one is one yes yes yes yes yes
3. Parts can be skipped no no partly yes partly yes yes partly
4. Inject at any stage no partly no partly partly yes yes no
5. Configurable no no no partly yes yes partly no
6. Library yes yes no yes yes Rust only in‑tree only yes
7. Serializable IR no yes yes yes partly yes yes, per build yes
8. IR assembled at runtime no no no partly partly yes yes no
9. Windows, Linux, macOS Windows yes no Linux yes yes yes yes yes
10. Fast, reentrant yes yes, per compiler instance is a process yes yes yes yes yes, one global session per thread
Yes / partly 2 / 1 3 / 2 1 / 2 7 / 3 5 / 5 8 / 2 6 / 4 5 / 2

A few notes on each.

FXC is one function, D3DCompile: HLSL in, DXBC out, nothing in between for you. Closed, Windows only, frozen at Shader Model 5.1. Close to zero on the list, and exactly what ideal 2 is for.

DXC is LLVM 3.7 with an HLSL front‑end, so everything on my list exists inside it and almost none of it is reachable: IDxcOptimizer runs passes by name, and that is it. One 18MB DLL, whether you want the SPIR‑V back‑end or not. That back‑end matters, though. With Glslang’s HLSL front‑end on its way out, DXC is where HLSL for Vulkan is headed.

Metal compiler is Clang. metal compiles MSL to AIR, which is LLVM bitcode, as a command line tool and nothing else; the only in‑process Metal compiler is the one inside the OS. Apple ships it for macOS and Windows, not Linux.

Glslang+SPIRV‑Tools+SPIRV‑Cross does ideal 1 in full, and is the best at 3 by accident: three libraries by three sets of authors with a binary format between them, so every seam is a place to stop or to insert your own. The price is the same fact from the other side: nobody owns the whole, and a front‑end can be deprecated without the back‑end noticing. For HLSL the optimizer is not optional; what Glslang emits is not legal SPIR‑V until SPIRV‑Tools has legalized it. More on that in the benchmark.

Tint has a proper IR, a builder, transforms, and compile‑time switches for every reader and writer, which on paper covers ideals 4, 5 and 8. In practice it is internal C++ with no stability promise, built by Dawn, and the public header tint.h offers Initialize, Shutdown and SpirvToWgsl. No optimizer, by design. Its SPIR‑V reader does not feed the writers directly but round‑trips through a WGSL AST; remember this for the benchmark.

Naga is the closest to the list. naga::Module is plain public data: build it by hand, walk it, rewrite it, hand it to any back‑end. Every front‑end and back‑end can be compiled out, the module serializes, and front‑end, validator and back‑ends are separate calls. What it lacks is an optimizer and a C API. What comes out is legal and unoptimized; if you want it optimized, something else has to do it. It is written in Rust, and from C++ that means writing a C wrapper around its types yourself, and fixing it every time Naga changes them, which is often. For a Rust project it is the answer. For me it is ideal 6 with a giant asterisk: for a C++ project it is close to non‑viable.

NIR is the IR inside every Mesa driver and Microsoft’s OpenCL and OpenGL layers on Direct3D 12, which makes it the most used shader compiler there is, and it has most of what my list asks for, built for a driver’s needs rather than mine. Passes are C functions called in any order, nir_builder builds IR by hand, nir_serialize writes it out, and there is a real optimizer. Faith Ekstrand’s In defense of NIR explains why it is built this way. SPIR‑V and GLSL come in; SPIR‑V, DXIL and MSL come out, next to the hardware back‑ends. None of it is a library: no public header, no stable API, no release, and the serialized form is for the build that wrote it. Each writer was written for one driver; the MSL one would not run without the driver’s descriptor lowering, so it is missing from the benchmark.

Slang is the only one designed as a whole compiler for more than one target: its own front‑end, IR, passes and writers, a proper API, every platform, and modules stored as serialized IR. It takes ideal 2 most seriously: FXC, DXC and the rest are “downstream compilers” it knows how to call, with a pass‑through mode that hands them the source untouched. What it lacks is the middle of my list: the IR is internal, with no API to read, transform or build it. And it comes as one piece: slang-compiler.dll is 26MB, plus a 6MB Glslang and SPIRV‑Tools for SPIR‑V.

Benchmark

There is a shader translation benchmark from 2022, by Naga’s author, in‑process and with I/O excluded, in which Naga won every round by an order of magnitude. It is four years old; these are today’s numbers.

Corpus. Every vertex, fragment and compute shader from the bgfx examples: 368 shaders, 120 vertex, 203 fragment and 45 compute, from a four‑line vertex shader to FSR and ASSAO. The same shaders exist in every language the compilers take:

  • HLSL, 316K lines. Every shader starts with the same thousand lines of helper functions, most of which it never calls, and every compiler parses them again for every shader.
  • SPIR‑V, optimized, 1.9MB.
  • WGSL, 41K lines, and MSL, 37K lines.

Method. One C++ executable links Glslang, SPIRV‑Tools, SPIRV‑Cross and Tint statically, and loads d3dcompiler_47.dll and dxcompiler.dll. Naga gets its own Rust executable, and Slang is used through the DLLs from its release package. Shaders are loaded into memory first, every compile runs 10 times (5 for Slang), the fastest run counts, and the result is the sum over the corpus. Single thread. Metal has no library, so it is one process per shader, best of 3, with process startup measured separately.

Versions. Glslang 16.1.0, SPIRV‑Tools v2025.5 and Tint as pinned by Dawn 4b91cc492; SPIRV‑Cross from August 2026; Naga 30.0.1; Slang v2026.19; DXC 1.10.2605; FXC 10.0.26100; Metal 32023.850; Mesa e2ab668. FXC and DXC at -O3, SPIRV‑Tools with its legalization and performance passes, Slang at its defaults, Tint driven the way its command line tool does it, Mesa through spirv_to_nir, then the passes and SPIR‑V writer of Zink, its OpenGL‑on‑Vulkan driver, or spirv_to_dxil. MSVC release builds, Ryzen 9 7950X, Windows 10.

Source to something a driver accepts

Every number here is all 368 shaders of the corpus, each compiled on its own to what its API’s driver loads, best of ten runs, summed.

Path Compiled Total Median per shader Slowest shader
Naga WGSL → SPIR‑V 368 0.22s 85µs 39ms
Tint WGSL → SPIR‑V 368 0.64s 408µs 94ms
Glslang+SPIRV‑Tools HLSL → SPIR‑V 368 4.96s 3.4ms 915ms
DXC HLSL → DXIL 368 5.99s 11.3ms 269ms
DXC HLSL → SPIR‑V 366 8.56s 10.6ms 1053ms
Slang HLSL → WGSL 360 13.53s 32.7ms 102ms
Slang HLSL → HLSL 368 13.53s 32.5ms 100ms
Slang HLSL → MSL 366 13.68s 32.9ms 100ms
Slang HLSL → GLSL 368 13.71s 32.4ms 104ms
Slang HLSL → SPIR‑V 368 14.70s 33.4ms 183ms
FXC HLSL → DXBC 368 15.43s 4.8ms 4088ms
Metal MSL → AIR 368 22.37s 56.5ms 325ms

Naga and Tint are in a different race. Neither reads HLSL, so they start from WGSL, and neither optimizes; they translate. What comes out needs no SPIRV‑Tools either: all 368 of Tint’s modules pass the validator as emitted, 366 of Naga’s do, the other two failing on a layout decoration on a workgroup array. Driver‑ready SPIR‑V comes out of Naga in 0.22s for the whole corpus and out of Tint in 0.64s. The rest of the table starts at 5s.

Glslang is fast, SPIRV‑Tools is not, and Glslang on its own is not enough. Parsing 316K lines of HLSL and emitting SPIR‑V takes Glslang 0.93s, 2.1ms per shader. But Glslang’s own help warns that -Od disables optimization; may cause illegal SPIR-V for HLSL, and it does: 173 of the 368 modules fail the validator until SPIRV‑Tools has legalized them, and none after. So the two are a pair, and the pair takes 4.96s. Legalizing and optimizing is 81% of that. HLSL to MSL through the whole stack, Glslang, SPIRV‑Tools, SPIRV‑Cross, takes 5.1s, and the optimizer is 79% of it.

FXC is two compilers. Its median is 4.8ms, less than half of DXC’s. Its total is 2.5 times DXC’s. Three shaders from one example take 4.1s, 2.9s and 1.6s, more than the other 365 put together. The same example has the slowest shaders for DXC, SPIRV‑Tools, SPIRV‑Cross and Tint too, but there the worst case stays around a second. This is the FXC everybody who shipped a D3D11 game remembers.

DXC is LLVM, and it shows. Its floor is 11ms, for a shader Glslang and SPIRV‑Tools together finish in 3ms. And DXC to SPIR‑V is the same job as Glslang+SPIRV‑Tools, HLSL in, optimized SPIR‑V out: DXC takes 8.6s, Glslang and the optimizer 5.0s. DXC also failed two compute shaders that it compiles to DXIL without complaint, and that Glslang compiles to SPIR‑V.

Slang is the slowest way from HLSL to SPIR‑V. Three times the Khronos stack, 1.7 times DXC. Almost none of it depends on the target: printing HLSL back out costs the same 33ms per shader as emitting SPIR‑V. The time is in the front‑end. A one‑line vertex shader goes through in 0.5ms, so the 30ms is the thousand lines of helper functions in front of every shader, which Slang checks whether the shader calls them or not. On the other hand it has no bad day: its slowest shader is 183ms, where FXC, DXC and SPIRV‑Tools each have one around a second or more.

Slang is also stricter than the HLSL compilers. None of the 368 shaders compiled as they were, so the HLSL was edited until they did. FXC, DXC and Glslang accept all of this, Slang does not:

  • A static global struct holding a sampler and a texture is “global variable cannot have opaque type”. 166 shaders; a macro that builds the struct where it is used gets around it.
  • A texel offset passed through a helper into SampleLevel or Load has to be constexpr, even in a function nobody calls, which rejects every shader that includes the helper.
  • min16float and friends don’t exist.
  • Two for (int k ...) loops in one function are an ambiguous k.
  • When the output is WGSL, fragment outputs have to be returned in a struct; an out float4 color : SV_TARGET0 parameter on the entry point is “system value semantic not supported”.

With those five edits to the shaders, Slang compiles all 368 to SPIR‑V, GLSL and HLSL, 366 to MSL, and 360 to WGSL. What is left are things the target doesn’t have, like InterlockedAdd in WGSL.

Metal is a process. Starting metal and doing nothing costs 10ms. Take that out and it is still 47ms per shader, 18.7s for the corpus, on the easiest input of the lot: 37K lines of machine‑written MSL against the 316K lines of HLSL the others chew through.

SPIR‑V in, SPIR‑V out, optimizer in between

NIR and SPIRV‑Tools do the same job here: take the SPIR‑V Glslang emits with optimization off, optimize it, write SPIR‑V. Naga and Tint are in the table for scale; they translate the optimized corpus and optimize nothing.

Input Compiled Total Median per shader Slowest shader
Naga SPIR‑V, optimized 358 0.03s 36µs 2ms
Tint SPIR‑V, optimized 359 0.97s 720µs 128ms
Mesa, NIR SPIR‑V, unoptimized 368 3.80s 169µs 1111ms
SPIRV‑Tools SPIR‑V, unoptimized 368 4.03s 1.23ms 909ms
Mesa, NIR → DXIL SPIR‑V, unoptimized 366 7.12s 472µs 2160ms

NIR’s optimizer is seven times cheaper per shader and costs the same in total. The median shader spends 169µs in NIR and 1.23ms in SPIRV‑Tools. Reading SPIR‑V is 41ms of Mesa’s 3.80s and writing it is 40ms; everything else is lowering and the optimizer loop. But 3.55s of it goes to the 20 shaders of one example, 54-s2h, where SPIRV‑Tools spends 2.79s. On the other 348 shaders NIR is done in 0.17s and SPIRV‑Tools needs 1.24s.

From HLSL, Glslang+NIR is the Khronos pipeline with Mesa’s optimizer in the middle. Same HLSL, same front‑end, NIR where SPIRV‑Tools was: 4.74s to SPIR‑V against 4.96s, and 8.04s to DXIL against DXC’s 5.99s from HLSL directly.

What comes out is written for a driver. Zink has NIR scalarize everything and leaves the vectors to the driver underneath, so the output is 8.1MB for the corpus against SPIRV‑Tools’ 1.9MB, and the s2h gather shader goes in at 72KB and comes out at 1.3MB. It is also not legal: the validator rejects 300 of the 368 modules, each on a uniform block with a matrix and no MatrixStride. The writer’s native Vulkan mode is new this year, and nothing ships against it yet.

DXIL is the long way round. spirv_to_dxil is the compiler of Dozen, Mesa’s Vulkan driver on top of Direct3D 12, as a library that WebGPU on Direct3D 12 uses too: SPIR‑V to NIR, then NIR to LLVM bitcode written by hand, without LLVM. Two shaders failed, one on SPV_EXT_shader_viewport_index_layer, which Dozen does not advertise, and one that crashed the writer.

SPIR‑V to source

Totals are over the 358 shaders that Naga, SPIRV‑Cross and Tint could all translate to all targets. Mesa appears for the one thing it writes:

SPIR‑V to Naga SPIRV‑Cross Tint Mesa (with optimizer)
MSL 38ms 152ms 1005ms -
HLSL 33ms 152ms 1095ms -
GLSL 31ms 148ms 1133ms -
WGSL 30ms - 787ms -
SPIR‑V 30ms - 970ms 2426ms
Median per shader, MSL 45µs 87µs 730µs -

Naga is 4x faster than SPIRV‑Cross and 26x faster than Tint. In 2022 it was 10x and 80x. The order has not changed and the gaps are smaller, but with a different corpus on a different machine that is all it says: the others may have got faster, or Naga slower.

Tint’s number is the round trip. SPIR‑V to IR, IR to WGSL AST, AST back to IR, IR to target. Printing WGSL, where it stops halfway, is its fastest path, and still 5x slower than SPIRV‑Cross at anything.

Not all SPIR‑V is welcome. SPIRV‑Cross took all 368 shaders for GLSL, HLSL and MSL. Tint rejected 9: eight use ImageGatherExtended and one SPV_EXT_shader_viewport_index_layer. Naga rejected the same 9, and panicked in its SPIR‑V front‑end on a tenth. By design: both read the subset of SPIR‑V that maps onto WGSL, not Vulkan’s SPIR‑V.

WGSL to everything

The comparison Tint and Naga were built for. Totals over the 365 shaders that both could translate to all targets:

WGSL to Naga Tint
IR, parsed and validated 201ms 431ms
SPIR‑V 221ms 629ms
MSL 224ms 663ms
HLSL 221ms 741ms
GLSL 218ms 779ms
Median per shader, SPIR‑V 84µs 407µs

From WGSL, Naga is about 3x faster than Tint, against 13x in 2022. Most of the difference is in the front‑ends: Naga spends 201ms parsing and validating WGSL it reads from SPIR‑V in 30ms. Once the module exists, writing it out costs Naga around 20ms for any target and Tint 200-350ms. Tint accepted all 368. Naga’s GLSL writer panicked on three compute shaders.

Binary size

The other half of ideal 6: the size of an executable that does the compiles above and nothing else:

What is in it Size
Naga SPIR‑V reader, WGSL writer 1.3MB
Glslang GLSL and HLSL front‑ends, SPIR‑V writer 2.1MB
SPIRV‑Cross GLSL, HLSL and MSL back‑ends 2.1MB
Naga WGSL reader, SPIR‑V writer 2.2MB
SPIRV‑Tools optimizer 2.8MB
Naga everything 3.7MB
FXC d3dcompiler_47.dll 4.7MB
Tint SPIR‑V reader, WGSL writer 5.3MB
Khronos stack Glslang+SPIRV‑Tools+SPIRV‑Cross 7.0MB
Tint everything 8.0MB
Mesa SPIR‑V reader, NIR with optimizer, SPIR‑V writer 8.6MB
Mesa SPIR‑V reader, NIR with optimizer, DXIL writer 9.0MB
DXC dxcompiler.dll + dxil.dll 19.7MB
Slang slang-compiler.dll+slang.dll+slang-glslang.dll 32.3MB
Metal metal.exe alone 119MB

Configurable means different things. Naga with one reader and one writer is a third of Naga with everything. Tint with one reader and one writer is still two thirds of Tint with everything, and four times Naga doing the same job. The Khronos stack is configurable by leaving a whole library out, which is coarse but works: SPIR‑V to MSL is SPIRV‑Cross alone, about 2MB; HLSL to SPIR‑V is Glslang plus the optimizer it cannot do without, about 5MB.

All of Naga is smaller than FXC. Five back‑ends, three front‑ends and a validator, in less space than one closed‑source HLSL compiler from 2012.

NIR’s size is its optimizer. Of the 8.6MB, 7MB is read‑only data, almost all of it the match tables nir_opt_algebraic generates from its Python rule files. The reader and the writer are a few hundred kilobytes each. An optimizer is the one thing Naga lacks, and in Mesa it is 7MB of the binary.

Conclusion

None of them is the ideal shader compiler. The API compilers, FXC, DXC and Metal, are ideal 2 and nothing else: black boxes, one to three orders of magnitude slower than the translators. The Khronos stack is modular because it is three projects, which also means three sets of bugs and a deprecated HLSL front‑end, and it is still the fastest way from HLSL to SPIR‑V. Slang has the API and the targets, and an IR with no API to it. Naga is the fastest, the smallest, the most configurable, and the only one with a public IR, it has no optimizer, and it is written in Rust. NIR has the optimizer and a public IR, but it is not a library anyone can grab and add to a project.

In Khronos’ 2026 shader ecosystem survey (Q11, “Would a Higher‑Level Shader IR Benefit Your Project?”, pages 26 and 27), nearly half of the respondents said their project would benefit from a standardized IR above SPIR‑V. An IR on its own is not much use; it needs a compiler around it, and that compiler is what the list above describes. None of it would have to be invented: every item on the list is implemented by somebody, and eight of ten by Naga alone. Nobody has put all ten in one library… Yet! 😉

References

  • Shader translation benchmark
    https://kvark.github.io/naga/shader/2022/02/17/shader-translation-benchmark.html

  • 2026 Real‑Time Shading Ecosystem Survey Report
    https://members.khronos.org/document/dl/36688

  • In defense of NIR
    https://www.gfxstrand.net/faith/blog/2022/01/in-defense-of-nir/

item.title: The bgfx shader compiler, 14 years of not being a compiler
item.description:
Introduction

bgfx renders through many backends, and each of them wants shaders in its own language: HLSL for Direct3D, Metal Shading Language on Apple platforms, GLSL for OpenGL and ESSL for OpenGL ES, SPIR-V for Vulkan, WGSL for WebGPU, etc. Nobody wants to write and maintain one shader per API. So bgfx has a shader compiler, shaderc, that takes a single source written in bgfx’s GLSL-flavoured dialect and produces a binary blob for whichever backend you ask for.

shaderc is the jankiest part of bgfx. I’ll say that upfront, because the rest of this post explains why it is janky, why it still works after fourteen years, and why I haven’t replaced it. It is not a compiler in the textbook sense. There is no parser, no AST, no IR of its own. It is a C preprocessor, a pile of #defines, textual patching of the source, and then a hand-off to somebody else’s real compiler. The price is that every target reports errors in its own way. The benefit is that adding a new target has never required touching a front-end, because there isn’t one. The language you write is GLSL. For every target that is not OpenGL, the text that actually gets compiled is HLSL.

shaderc was in the initial commit of bgfx, on 3 April 2012, as a single tools/shaderc.cpp of 664 lines. It came with two third-party dependencies, both of which outlived every other decision made that day: fcpp, a C preprocessor with roots in 1984, and glsl-optimizer, an extraction of Mesa’s GLSL compiler.

Android and Native Client got GLSL through glsl-optimizer. Windows and Xbox 360 got HLSL through D3DXCompileShader from the D3DX9 library:

The output container from that first version, a uniform table (name, type, count, register) followed by the shader blob, is still the same shape today, just with more fields.

How does it work?

Take the simplest example in the repo, vs_cubes.sc:

 1$input a_position, a_color0
 2$output v_color0
 3
 4#include "../common/common.sh"
 5
 6void main()
 7{
 8	gl_Position = mul(u_modelViewProj, vec4(a_position, 1.0) );
 9	v_color0 = a_color0;
10}

Next to it sits varying.def.sc, which is the only place where types and semantics of inputs and outputs are declared:

1vec4 v_color0    : COLOR0    = vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
2
3vec3 a_position  : POSITION;
4vec4 a_color0    : COLOR0;

A typical compile looks like this:

shaderc -f vs_cubes.sc --type vertex --platform windows -p s_5_0 -i src -o vs_cubes.bin

Then compiling it takes these steps:

1. Preprocess, first pass. The source goes through the C preprocessor once, with the platform, language and shader type defines set, so that includes are pulled in and any #if around the $input and $output lines is resolved.

2. Parse the $input and $output lines. These are not preprocessor directives. shaderc reads them off the top of the preprocessed text and strips them. They list which of the varyings from varying.def.sc this shader uses. shaderc also hashes the sorted list so that at runtime bgfx can verify a vertex shader’s outputs match a fragment shader’s inputs.

3. Build a preamble. This is where the target language is decided, and it is done by generating text and prepending it to the source. For HLSL-family targets the preamble starts with the type aliases:

 1	preprocessor.writef(
 2		"#define lowp\n"
 3		"#define mediump\n"
 4		"#define highp\n"
 5		"#define ivec2 int2\n"
 6		"#define ivec3 int3\n"
 7		"#define ivec4 int4\n"
 8		"#define uvec2 uint2\n"
 9		"#define uvec3 uint3\n"
10		"#define uvec4 uint4\n"
11		"#define vec2 float2\n"
12		"#define vec3 float3\n"
13		"#define vec4 float4\n"
14		"#define mat2 float2x2\n"
15		"#define mat3 float3x3\n"
16		"#define mat4 float4x4\n"
17		);

And then the actual trick. GLSL has void main() with globals for inputs and outputs. HLSL wants an entry point with typed, semantic-annotated parameters and a return struct. shaderc generates a macro for that from the varyings, roughly for the vertex shader above:

 1struct Output
 2{
 3	vec4 gl_Position : SV_POSITION;
 4#define gl_Position _varying_.gl_Position
 5	vec4 v_color0 : COLOR0;
 6#define v_color0 _varying_.v_color0
 7};
 8#define void_main() \
 9Output main( \
10	vec3 a_position : POSITION \
11	, vec4 a_color0 : COLOR0 \
12	) \
13{ \
14	Output _varying_; \
15	v_color0 = vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
16#define __RETURN__ \
17	} \
18	return _varying_

The vec3 and vec4 in there are fine, because the type aliases above turn them into float3 and float4 on the way through. smooth and flat from varying.def.sc are rewritten to linear and nointerpolation while the struct is being generated.

4. Patch the source. The shader still says void main(). shaderc finds it and overwrites one byte, the space, with an underscore, so it now reads void_main() and expands to the macro above. For vertex shaders it then finds the closing brace of main and inserts __RETURN__; in front of it. That is the entire “translation” of the entry point: one byte and one string insert.

1	*const_cast<char*>(entry.getPtr() + 4) = '_';

The fragment shader side is the same idea, except main stays void and outputs become out parameters. gl_FragColor becomes bgfx_FragData0 : SV_TARGET0, gl_FragCoord becomes a SV_POSITION parameter, gl_FrontFacing is SV_IsFrontFace. Which of these get added to the signature is decided by searching the source text for the identifier.

5. Preprocess, second pass. The preamble plus the patched source go through the preprocessor again, and this time the macros do their work. void_main() expands, vec4 becomes float4, and bgfx_shader.sh, which the shader included through common.sh, supplies the rest. That header is where SAMPLER2D, texture2D, mul, mtxFromRows, vec4_splat and friends are defined per language. For HLSL it wraps texture and sampler pairs into structs so that GLSL-style texture2D(s_tex, uv) works; for GLSL it defines mul(a, b) as a * b. The header, not the compiler, is where most of the language knowledge lives:

1// HLSL
2#define SAMPLER2D(_name, _reg) \
3	uniform SamplerState _name ## Sampler : REGISTER(s, _reg); \
4	uniform Texture2D    _name ## Texture : REGISTER(t, _reg); \
5	static BgfxSampler2D _name = { _name ## Sampler, _name ## Texture }
6
7// GLSL
8#define SAMPLER2D(_name, _reg) uniform sampler2D _name
9#define mul(_a, _b) ( (_a) * (_b) )

For vs_cubes.sc, after that pass, the entry point FXC sees is roughly:

 1struct Output
 2{
 3	float4 gl_Position : SV_POSITION;
 4	float4 v_color0 : COLOR0;
 5};
 6
 7Output main(float3 a_position : POSITION, float4 a_color0 : COLOR0)
 8{
 9	Output _varying_;
10	_varying_.v_color0 = float4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
11	_varying_.gl_Position = mul(u_modelViewProj, float4(a_position, 1.0) );
12	_varying_.v_color0 = a_color0;
13	return _varying_;
14}

Above that sits the rest of bgfx_shader.sh: built-in uniforms, mul, splat helpers, the lot. --preprocess dumps this text. When a target compiler complains, the code it is complaining about is this, not the .sc you wrote.

6. Hand it to a real compiler. The preprocessed text is now legal GLSL or legal HLSL, and it goes to FXC, DXC, Glslang, or whatever the profile wants. What comes back is the shader binary. Uniform and sampler reflection is taken from the compiler that produced it: D3DReflect after FXC, DXC’s reflection blob after DXIL, Glslang’s live uniforms or SPIRV-Cross resources after anything that went through SPIR-V. shaderc writes that into its own container, ahead of the shader blob, together with the $input and $output hashes from step 2.

Before and after glsl-optimizer

This is what shaderc looked like just before the glsl-optimizer removal in August 2026, with every target it had accumulated:

The left side is the legacy. glsl-optimizer’s front-end was Mesa as of the mid-2010s, and it never implemented GLSL 4.x, so anything above 4.00 (and ESSL above 3.00) had, since 2017, been passed through untouched. In practice that meant a GLSL 4.30 shader got no validation at all at build time. You found out it was broken when the driver rejected it at runtime, on whichever machine happened to run it first. Meanwhile every extension needed on the GLSL side was detected by grepping the source for identifiers and prepending #extension lines. glsl-optimizer would then add its own EXT and ARB suffixes to the functions those extensions provide, which had to be patched back out so that the same shader would load across GLSL and ESSL versions, and the runtime would re-add whatever the driver actually needed.

After removing glsl-optimizer and raising the minimum API versions on OpenGL to 4.3 and OpenGL ES to 3.0, and replacing fcpp with a preprocessor of my own, this is how the compiler looks today:

Every target now has a validated front-end; every target except FXC and DXC produces SPIR-V on the way. The GLSL / HLSL fork is still there: a shader can compile as spirv and fail as 430, because those are not the same program.

Could it be simpler?

If you look carefully at the diagram, you might notice that the GLSL and HLSL patching could be unified, because Glslang accepts HLSL and SPIRV-Cross is already used to output GLSL/ESSL. This would simplify the preprocessor macros and the patching, but having two paths keeps some flexibility for when a new shader language needs to be added, which doesn’t happen often.

Another thing that might not be obvious is that the bgfx shader language could simply be HLSL. Some of the bgfx shaping happens with preprocessor macros, but it’s feasible to do that transformation inside Glslang traversers, with plain HLSL as the front-end. It might look like the obvious choice to switch the default bgfx shader language to HLSL.

The problem is that this would tie shaderc to Glslang even further, and I don’t control where Glslang goes. This is not hypothetical. In April 2026 Glslang proposed deprecating and removing its HLSL front-end, and the README now reads:

The HLSL front-end is deprecated as of April 2026 and will be removed at the next major version of glslang. […] Projects that require continued HLSL support should maintain a fork of glslang at the tag corresponding to the deprecation announcement.

Had the bgfx shader language been HLSL, every existing shader would now need to move. Because the language is GLSL and HLSL is only an intermediate, the exposure is limited to the spirv, metal and wgsl paths, and those can be moved to another HLSL compiler, or to the GLSL front-end, without touching a single .sc file.

It cuts the other way too. The WGSL path exists only because I carry a stripped-down copy of Tint for one translation, SPIR-V to WGSL. SPIRV-Cross already does SPIR-V to GLSL, ESSL and MSL for me, so in January 2026 I asked whether it could do WGSL as well and let me drop Tint. The maintainer’s answer:

I don’t have bandwidth to implement and maintain yet another backend. There is also no motivation to effectively duplicate the effort that Tint already does.

Fair enough on bandwidth. But SPIRV-Cross is not one person’s side project, it is a Khronos project, and WGSL is a W3C standard implemented in every major browser. If the “Cross” in SPIRV-Cross is understood as “to every shading language”, this is Khronos declining to cross to one of them, and pointing at Google’s compiler instead. That is the whole reason shaderc looks the way it does. Every project in the pipeline solves its own problem, none of them shares bgfx’s vision, and nobody is obliged to. The Frankenstein is not a design choice. It is what you get when you assemble a compiler from parts whose owners don’t answer to you, and the seams between them are yours to maintain.

glsl-optimizer was a great idea!

glsl-optimizer was built for Unity 3.0, where it made mobile shaders faster on drivers whose own compilers did little or no optimization. bgfx picked it up for the same reason: in 2012 the GLSL targets were Android and Native Client, and the shader compilers behind those were not something you wanted to trust with unoptimized code.

It is simple. The library is Mesa’s GLSL front-end, Mesa’s IR, Mesa’s optimization passes, and one file, ir_print_glsl_visitor.cpp, that walks the IR and prints GLSL. Metal support, when it came, was a second printer, ir_print_metal_visitor.cpp. The public API is a dozen C functions in one header, and the ones you need are initialize, optimize, get status, get log, get output, cleanup. The initial shaderc.cpp used it in 30 lines.

The code is clear. Mesa’s GLSL IR is a plain tree of ir_instruction nodes with a visitor.

It outputs source. This is the property I want to underline, because it is the one that mattered most and the one that is rarest. Most shader compilers produce an IR that a driver consumes: DXBC, DXIL, SPIR-V. Or there is no optimizer, because text is always treated as source, and there is no split between text as source and text as IR. glsl-optimizer showed, in 2010, that the sane way to deal with text as an interchange format is not to ship the shader as the author wrote it, but to run it through a real compiler with real optimization passes and print the result: the minimum code required for the shader, with every dead uniform and unreachable branch already gone. I made this same argument in the WebGPU post when defending WGSL as textual IR; glsl-optimizer is where I got this “aha” moment about how shader code/text should be treated.

Why it had to go. Its author stopped working on it in mid-2016 when Unity moved to a proper (proprietary) shader compiler. Mesa has since moved its optimization work to NIR, so the GLSL IR that glsl-optimizer is built on is no longer maintained upstream either. It’s a dead project.

What makes shaderc janky?

In a 2014 survey of cross platform shaders, bgfx was the example of the first, and least sophisticated, approach on the list:

Write some helper macros to abstract away HLSL & GLSL differences, and make everyone aware of all the differences.

Twelve years later that is still what shaderc is, with real compilers bolted on behind the macros. A commenter on Hacker News put it more bluntly, in a thread about shader compilation for SDL_GPU:

BGFX uses a different approach. You basically write your shader in a GLSL-like language but it’s all just (either very clever or very horrible) macro expansions that handles all the platform differences. With that you get a very performant backend for OpenGL, WebGL, Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D 11 and 12 and Playstation. It’s shader compiler program basically does minimal source level transformations before handing it over to the platforms’ own shader compiler if available.

I’ll take “either”.

Error messages depend on the target. A shader that fails on s_5_0 gives you an FXC error. The same shader on spirv gives you a Glslang error, on metal a Glslang error followed possibly by a SPIRV-Cross assertion, on wgsl any of those plus a Tint diagnostic, and on 430 a Glslang error in the GLSL dialect. They report different line numbers, because each one is looking at a different preamble prepended to your code. shaderc tries to help by printing the patched source around the reported line, but you still have to know which tool is talking.

Features are detected by substring. Whether gl_FragDepth appears in the source decides whether SV_DEPTH goes into the signature.

The entry point is a macro. For a vertex shader, everything about main is done by rewriting one byte and inserting __RETURN__ before the last brace. An early return; inside a vertex shader’s main is a compile error, because main now returns Output. The docs say attributes and varyings can only be accessed from main(), and now you know why: outside main there is no _varying_ to expand to.

The dialect is real. SAMPLER2D(s_tex, 0) instead of uniform sampler2D, vec4_splat(x) instead of vec4(x), mul(a, b) instead of a * b, mtxFromRows instead of a matrix constructor, etc. Each of those exists because the two sides disagree and the preprocessor cannot resolve the disagreement without a hint from you.

How do others do it?

The alternatives I have seen in other open source libraries and engines do not do much better. Most take a similar Frankenstein approach: a shader compiler assembled from parts of other shader compilers, written by different teams with different goals. Here is how the ones I know of get from what you write to what the GPU driver accepts, sorted into four groups by how much of the job they actually do themselves.

Janky. Text goes in, gets transformed, and is handed to whichever compiler the target uses. Each of those compilers is free to accept or reject the result on its own terms, so the same source can pass on one API and fail on another. That is the jank, and this is the shaderc family:

You write How it gets there Outputs
bgfx shaderc GLSL dialect + macros preprocessor + text patching → FXC / DXC / Glslang → SPIRV-Cross / Tint DXBC, DXIL, SPIR-V, GLSL, ESSL, MSL, WGSL, PSSL
The Forge FSL, an HLSL superset Python translator emits per-platform source → DXC / Glslang / metal / psslc DXIL, SPIR-V, metallib, PSSL
Magnum GLSL runtime #define assembly per GL version, Glslang plugin GLSL, SPIR-V
Diligent Engine HLSL (also GLSL, MSL, WGSL) own HLSL→GLSL text converter for OpenGL; FXC / DXC, Glslang → SPIR-V, Tint → WGSL elsewhere DXBC, DXIL, GLSL, SPIR-V, MSL, WGSL
Flax Engine HLSL FXC for SM5, DXC for SM6, Glslang HLSL front-end → SPIR-V DXBC, DXIL, SPIR-V

Text translators. One parser of their own, one set of emitters of their own, and nothing you would call an optimizer in between. They print what you wrote in the target’s language and let the driver’s compiler do the rest. All three exist because a browser needed to compile somebody else’s shading language safely:

You write How it gets there Outputs
Dawn / Tint WGSL (also SPIR-V in) own readers → Tint IR → own writers, legalization and dead code elimination only, no optimizer SPIR-V, MSL, HLSL, GLSL, WGSL
wgpu / Naga WGSL (also GLSL, SPIR-V in) own front-ends → Naga IR → own back-ends, constant evaluation and pruning only SPIR-V, MSL, HLSL, GLSL, WGSL
ANGLE GLSL ES own translator → own AST → own back-ends, AST clean-up only, no SPIRV-Tools HLSL, GLSL, SPIR-V, MSL, WGSL

A real front-end. One compiler parses and validates the source, so an error is the same error no matter which backend you asked for, and one source really does target every backend. What happens after that is somebody else’s back-end: usually SPIR-V as the interchange format and SPIRV-Cross or Tint printing whatever the target wants. Some of these have a parser of their own in front (Godot, O3DE, Stride), but it only produces text for the next tool in line:

You write How it gets there Outputs
sokol-shdc Vulkan GLSL 450 + @ tags Glslang → SPIRV-Tools → SPIRV-Cross / Tint SPIR-V, GLSL, ESSL, HLSL, MSL, WGSL
SDL_GPU (SDL_shadercross) HLSL or SPIR-V DXC → DXIL / SPIR-V, FXC → DXBC, SPIRV-Cross → MSL DXBC, DXIL, SPIR-V, MSL
Filament ESSL 3.0 Glslang → SPIRV-Tools → SPIRV-Cross / Tint SPIR-V, GLSL, ESSL, MSL, WGSL
Godot 4 Godot shading language own parser emits GLSL → Glslang → SPIR-V → Mesa NIR → DXIL, SPIRV-Cross → MSL SPIR-V, DXIL, MSL, GLSL
O3DE AZSL, an HLSL superset mcpp → AZSLc → HLSL → DXC, SPIRV-Cross → MSL DXIL, SPIR-V, MSL
Stride SDSL, an HLSL superset own compiler → HLSL → FXC; SPIR-V pipeline in progress DXBC, SPIR-V, GLSL
Wicked Engine HLSL SM6 DXC → DXIL / SPIR-V, Metal Shader Converter → metallib DXBC, DXIL, SPIR-V, metallib
Veldrid Vulkan GLSL or SPIR-V Glslang → SPIR-V → SPIRV-Cross, at runtime HLSL, GLSL, ESSL, MSL
ShaderConductor HLSL DXC → SPIR-V → SPIRV-Cross (archived 2025) DXIL, SPIR-V, GLSL, ESSL, MSL

Actual compilers. Text in, optimization in the middle, and out comes whatever the API accepts, with no other compiler in between. Where the API accepts source, as OpenGL, Metal and WebGPU do, that source counts as the API’s IR. By that definition the list is short:

You write Straight to the API Still needs Optimization
Slang Slang SPIR-V, MSL, WGSL, GLSL DXC / FXC for DXIL / DXBC, NVRTC for PTX own IR passes (specialization, inlining, SSA, dead code), then SPIRV-Tools optimizer at -O1 and up
glsl-optimizer (2010-2016) GLSL GLSL, ESSL, MSL nothing Mesa’s GLSL IR passes

Slang qualifies everywhere except Direct3D, because nobody in these tables emits DXIL on their own. It is LLVM 3.7 bitcode that until 2025 had to be signed by Microsoft’s dxil.dll before a driver would accept it, and the one open source emitter I know of is Mesa’s nir_to_dxil, which is how Godot got there. glsl-optimizer is in the table because, for the one API it served, it was exactly this: parse, optimize, print what the driver accepts. The text translators above would qualify too if they optimized anything, and that is the situation glsl-optimizer was written to fix in 2010. The browsers have chosen to live with it.

Only the last group comes close to having no seam, and the one Slang keeps is Direct3D’s doing, not Slang’s. Everything above it hands text to a compiler someone else maintains. The real front-ends hide that better than shaderc does, at the cost of Glslang and SPIRV-Cross being load-bearing, which is exactly the exposure the HLSL front-end deprecation just demonstrated. None of them removes it, and the ones that look cleaner usually support fewer targets.

Conclusion

And yet it works! Fourteen years, eight target languages, every one of them added without a front-end rewrite. The structure that made this possible is the same one that makes the error messages inconsistent: shaderc owns the front of the pipeline, delegates the back, and the seam between them is text. Nearly everyone else in the tables above has that seam in the same place.

The one real newcomer in those tables is Slang. It is an actual compiler: a front-end, an IR, modules, generics, and code generation for HLSL, GLSL, SPIR-V, MSL, WGSL, and even Slang round-trip from one source. That is the set bgfx needs. It came out of NVIDIA research and has been hosted by Khronos since late 2024. The press release claims that “Valve compiled the entire production Source 2 HLSL codebase with Slang while modifying only 10 lines of code.” It is the first thing in this space that solves the problem instead of routing around it. It did not exist in 2012, which is why shaderc is a preprocessor and a hand-off. If this were started today, Slang would be the approach it would take.

item.title: Writing a C preprocessor for bgfx shader compiler
item.description:
Introduction

For 14+ years, every shader that bgfx compiled, starting from the initial commit, went through a preprocessor written for the Amiga with origins in 1984:

fcpp - Frexx CPP (C Preprocessor)

This is a C preprocessor. It is a project based on public domain code, then forked by Daniel in 1993 and future work has been done under a BSD license.

That public domain code is the DECUS cpp, written by Martin Minow in 1984–85. So the preprocessor bgfx shipped in 2026 had a code lineage reaching back forty years, by way of an Amiga port. The sources still carry REG(a0) register-parameter macros and #ifdef AMIGA blocks.

And it worked. This deserves emphasis, because the rest of this post is about replacing it. Over fourteen years fcpp needed only 25 commits’ worth of attention in the bgfx tree, most of them routine resyncs with upstream. For a dependency you are supposed to forget about, that is close to the ideal outcome.

What made it a good fit specifically was how configurable it was. fcpp exposes 37 FPPTAG_* options through a single entry point:

1int fppPreProcess(struct fppTag *tags);

shaderc used 13 of them: FPPTAG_INPUT and FPPTAG_OUTPUT to route all I/O through bgfx’s own file abstraction, FPPTAG_ERROR to capture diagnostics, FPPTAG_DEPENDS for makefile dependency output, plus FPPTAG_LINE, FPPTAG_KEEPCOMMENTS, FPPTAG_RIGHTCONCAT and others to shape the output. Crucially, fcpp keeps no global mutable state, everything lives in a struct Global allocated per call, and it never insists on calling fopen itself. Both properties are rarer than they should be, and both are exactly what an embedder wants. fcpp got the architecture right.

So what’s bad about it?

The code is crufty. It is K&R-flavoured C89 with 1980s conventions throughout, spread over six .c files with names that tell you nothing: cpp1.c through cpp6.c. State is threaded through a 250-line struct Global. Making a behavioural change means understanding a program written under constraints 512 KB of RAM, no function prototypes, that stopped applying decades ago.

Upstream is frozen. fcpp is not abandoned; Daniel Stenberg still merges the occasional PR. But the most recent one, in November 2025, is titled “tidy-up whitespace, fix warnings, potential overflow”. It is janitorial. There has been no functional development in many years. One detail captures the situation precisely. That November 2025 upstream commit fixes an sprintf buffer overflow in cpp3.c:

cpp3.c:336:28: warning: '%4d' directive writing between 4 and 11 bytes into
a region of size between 0 and 6 [-Wformat-overflow=]

bgfx had already fixed that exact bug locally in commit ab0a091, on 8 December 2018, seven years earlier. That is what a frozen dependency feels like from the outside: you carry local patches indefinitely, and upstream converges on your fix long after you forgot about it.

Why bgfx shader compiler needs preprocessor?

It is worth being clear about what that preprocessor is actually doing there, because it is not typical role that C preprocessor usually plays in C/C++ code. bgfx targets a dozen graphics APIs, and each comes with its own shading language: HLSL for Direct3D, Metal Shading Language on Apple platforms, GLSL and its embedded variant for OpenGL, SPIR-V for Vulkan, WGSL for WebGPU. They are close relatives, but they disagree constantly on details, how you declare a texture and its sampler, how you bind one to a register, how you multiply a matrix, what an entry point looks like. Rather than ask people to write and maintain one shader per API, bgfx has them write one bgfx’s GLSL-inspired style, then include a header at the top of it: bgfx_shader.sh for vertex and fragment shaders, bgfx_compute.sh for compute. Those headers are almost nothing but preprocessor, a few hundred macros and conditional branches that reshape that single source into whatever the target language expects, selected by defines the compiler sets per target. So the preprocessor is not a preliminary pass that strips comments before the real work begins, it is the portability layer, and every shader in every bgfx project goes through it.

What else is out there?

I looked at what else was out there to find a comparable replacement.

fcpp ucpp mcpp tinycpp tcpp Desired
Language C89 C89/C99 C89 C99 + POSIX C++14 C99 or C++20 (or below)
Core size 5,737 LOC 10,725 LOC 17,489 LOC 2,032 + 624 LOC 2,331 LOC ~2-3K LOC max
Files 6 .c + 7 .h 8 .c + 7 .h 7 .c + 5 .h 2 .c + 2 .h + 4 .h 1 .hpp 1 .cpp + 1 .h
Licence BSD-3 / MIT BSD-3 BSD-2 MIT (+ LGPL dep) Apache-2.0 Permissive
Last commit 2025-11 (janitorial) 2015 (archived) 2017 2020 2025-04 Active
Third-party deps none none none libulz (LGPL-2.1) none none
C++ STL no no no no heavy no
Custom allocator no no no no no yes
Global mutable state no yes yes no no no
Virtual filesystem partial no no no yes yes
Structured error callback yes opt-in text only no / stderr yes yes
Calls exit() no yes likely no no no
Variadic macros no yes yes yes no yes
Trigraphs / digraphs no yes yes no no Don’t care!

A few notes on each.

ucpp is the most standards-serious of the small ones, genuinely, fully C99, with trigraphs, digraphs, _Pragma and arbitrary-precision #if arithmetic. It is also the largest of them after mcpp: at 10,725 lines it is nearly twice fcpp and four times tinycpp, which is the price of that conformance. It is archived on GitHub, with its last commit in March 2015. It keeps preprocessor state in file-scope globals. That rules out two instances at once, which rules out ever compiling shaders on a thread pool. It also resolves #include by calling fopen itself, and its fatal path is die() → exit(1).

mcpp is the conformance champion, and is honest about it, the README claims “the highest conformance” and it ships a validation suite so respected that tinycpp’s author used it to test his own implementation. It is also 17,489 lines with an autoconf build, module-level global state, a mcpp_lib_main(int argc, char **argv) entry point that wants command-line arguments, and no way to intercept include resolution. It is a compiler component that grew a library mode, not a library. Last commit: 2017.

tinycpp is the closest in spirit to what I wanted. The smallest real implementation in the survey at 2,032 lines, MIT, with a clean opaque-handle API and no globals. Three things stopped us, and the first is fatal on its own. tinycpp is MIT, but it is not self-contained: it needs tglist.h and hbmap.h from libulz which is LGPL-2.1! Then its I/O is FILE*-shaped, and diagnostics go straight to stderr with no callback.

tcpp is aimed squarely at shader preprocessing, which makes it the most obvious candidate on paper, and it has the nicest embedding story of the lot: an IInputStream interface and a std::function include callback, so it never touches the filesystem. But it is a single 2,331-line header that includes <string>, <vector>, <list>, <unordered_map>, <unordered_set>, <sstream>, <functional>, <memory>, <algorithm>, <tuple> and <stack>. 🤮 Nope!

The pattern across all five: the ones with clean embedding stories are STL-heavy or unmaintained, the ones with real conformance are large and full of globals, the one that is small and well-designed drags in an LGPL dependency, and none of them let you supply an allocator.

Writing C preprocessor from scratch

shaderc::Preprocessor is around 3K lines of code across pp.cpp and pp.h. The public surface is deliberately tiny - its entire public surface is one callback interface and one class:

  1namespace shaderc
  2{
  3	/// Position in the source being preprocessed.
  4	///
  5	struct SourceLocation
  6	{
  7		/// Default constructor.
  8		///
  9		SourceLocation()
 10			: line(0) {}
 11
 12		/// Constructor with specific file, and line number.
 13		///
 14		SourceLocation(const bx::StringView& _file, uint32_t _line)
 15			: file(_file), line(_line) {}
 16
 17		bx::StringView file; //!< File the location is in.
 18		uint32_t       line; //!< One-based line number inside `file`.
 19	};
 20
 21	/// Host hooks for the preprocessor.
 22	///
 23	/// All file IO and diagnostics are routed through these so the engine itself never touches
 24	/// the filesystem and stays reentrant. One `Preprocessor` instance is one independent unit
 25	/// of work.
 26	///
 27	struct BX_NO_VTABLE PreprocessorCallbackI
 28	{
 29		///
 30		virtual ~PreprocessorCallbackI() = 0;
 31
 32		/// Resolve and read `#include`.
 33		///
 34		/// @param[in]  _name Include name, without quotes or angle brackets.
 35		/// @param[in]  _isSystem True for `<...>`, and false for `"..."`.
 36		/// @param[in]  _from File holding the directive, so that quoted include can be resolved
 37		///   relative to it.
 38		/// @param[out] _writer File text is written here. Preprocessor owns the storage, and
 39		///   copies it out before this call returns, so nothing has to outlive the call.
 40		/// @param[out] _outPath Resolved path, used for dependency reporting.
 41		/// @param[out] _err Error, set if writing file text fails.
 42		///
 43		/// @returns True if include is resolved and read, otherwise returns false.
 44		///
 45		virtual bool include(
 46			  const bx::StringView& _name
 47			, bool _isSystem
 48			, const bx::StringView& _from
 49			, bx::WriterI* _writer
 50			, bx::FilePath& _outPath
 51			, bx::Error* _err
 52			) = 0;
 53
 54		/// Reports file the output depends on. It's called for the main source, and for every
 55		/// opened include.
 56		///
 57		/// @param[in] _path Resolved path of the file.
 58		///
 59		/// @remarks Default implementation ignores dependencies.
 60		///
 61		virtual void depend(const bx::StringView& _path) = 0;
 62
 63		/// Diagnostic sink.
 64		///
 65		/// @param[in] _isError True for `#error` and hard failures, and false for `#warning`.
 66		/// @param[in] _location Source position the diagnostic originated from.
 67		/// @param[in] _message Diagnostic message.
 68		///
 69		virtual void message(
 70			  bool _isError
 71			, const SourceLocation& _location
 72			, const bx::StringView& _message
 73			) = 0;
 74	};
 75
 76	inline PreprocessorCallbackI::~PreprocessorCallbackI()
 77	{
 78	}
 79
 80	/// C-style preprocessor.
 81	///
 82	/// Supports object and function macros (including variadics and `__VA_OPT__`), `#` and `##`,
 83	/// `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#elif`, `#elifdef`, `#elifndef`, `#else`, `#endif`,
 84	/// `#include`, `#line`, `#pragma once`, `#error`, `#warning`, and `__LINE__`, `__FILE__` and
 85	/// `__COUNTER__`. There are no trigraphs or digraphs.
 86	///
 87	class Preprocessor
 88	{
 89		BX_CLASS(Preprocessor
 90			, NO_COPY
 91			);
 92
 93	public:
 94		/// Constructor.
 95		///
 96		/// @param[in] _callback Host hooks. It must outlive Preprocessor.
 97		/// @param[in] _allocator Allocator. It must not be NULL, and it must outlive
 98		///   Preprocessor.
 99		///
100		Preprocessor(PreprocessorCallbackI& _callback, bx::AllocatorI* _allocator);
101
102		/// Destructor.
103		///
104		~Preprocessor();
105
106		/// Predefine macro, mirroring `-D` command-line define.
107		///
108		/// @param[in] _define Macro in `NAME`, `NAME=VALUE`, or `NAME(a,b)=body` form.
109		///
110		void define(const bx::StringView& _define);
111
112		/// Remove predefined, or previously defined macro.
113		///
114		/// @param[in] _name Macro name.
115		///
116		void undefine(const bx::StringView& _name);
117
118		/// Emit `#line <line> "<file>"` directives into the output so that consumer can map the
119		/// result back to the original source.
120		///
121		/// @param[in] _emit True to emit `#line` directives.
122		///
123		/// @remarks It's off by default. Directives, skipped `#if` branches, and `#include` all
124		///   break 1:1 line mapping, so this is the only way to get meaningful positions, but it
125		///   requires consumer to understand `#line`.
126		///
127		void setEmitLineDirectives(bool _emit);
128
129		/// Preprocess source.
130		///
131		/// @param[in]  _name Source name, used for diagnostics and `__FILE__`.
132		/// @param[in]  _source Source to preprocess.
133		/// @param[out] _writer Result is written here.
134		/// @param[out] _err Error, set if writing result fails.
135		///
136		/// @returns True on success, or false if `#error`, or hard error was reported.
137		///
138		bool preprocess(
139			  const bx::StringView& _name
140			, const bx::StringView& _source
141			, bx::WriterI* _writer
142			, bx::Error* _err
143			);
144
145	private:
146		struct PreprocessorImpl* m_impl;
147	};
148
149} // namespace shaderc

That is the whole API. Compare it to fcpp’s 37 tags, of which we used 13 and ignored 24.

It supports #define, #undef, #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elif, #else, #endif, #include, #pragma, #error, #warning and #line; object and function macros including variadics; # and ##; and __LINE__ and __FILE__.

1. We do not care about full C99 conformance. Trigraphs and digraphs exist so that 1980s terminals lacking #, [ and { could write C.
